1.title: Find problems where quantum may help
1.intro: Quantum computers do not speed up everything. Your first job is to find problems where they may help and to say honestly where they will not.
pts: Quantum methods are studied for three families of problem: simulating molecules and materials, searching or optimising among huge numbers of choices, and some cryptography tasks.
Most office work, databases and web pages gain nothing from quantum hardware. A buyer who hears 'quantum' for these should be told so.
Ask of any problem: how many choices, how costly is a wrong answer, and what does the best classical method already achieve? Write the three answers before you propose anything.
Canadian buyers include research groups, banks, logistics firms and energy companies; write one concrete problem for each.
1.ex: Delivery routing for 40 stops has an astronomically large number of orders, but good classical heuristics already get within a few percent of best. Verdict: quantum is not yet worth the cost; recommend a classical solver and a watch list.
1.act: Write a one-page 'is it quantum?' screen for three real problems and give a verdict with the three answers for each.
1.std: Each verdict cites the classical baseline; at least one problem is rejected with reasons.

2.title: Know the rules, exports and standards in Canada
2.intro: Quantum technology is a controlled field. The rules decide who you may work with and what you may send abroad.
pts: Strategic technology can need a federal export permit; check the control list before you send code, designs or papers to another country.
Research funding and public contracts often require security screening of staff and a data-handling plan.
Cryptography guidance from the federal cyber agency sets timelines for moving to quantum-safe methods; track it.
Intellectual property: agree in writing who owns code and results when you work with a university or client.
2.ex: Row: 'Send circuit design to a partner abroad | federal export control | check list, ask for permit if listed | before first send | permit or written no-permit-needed note on file'.
2.act: Build the rules table for a 3-person quantum start-up in your province, with a source and date per row.
2.std: Every row has an enforcer, action and date; no rule guessed.

3.title: Build and run a small quantum program
3.intro: You learn by running real circuits on a simulator and on freely available cloud hardware, and recording what the noise does.
pts: A qubit holds a blend of 0 and 1 until measured. Measure many times ('shots') and you get a pattern of counts, not one answer.
Start with two circuits: a coin-flip (one gate) and an entangled pair (two gates). Predict the counts, then run them.
Compare simulator and real hardware: the hardware shows errors. Record the error rate as wrong counts divided by total shots.
Use version control; save the circuit, shots, device name, date and result in one table row per run.
3.ex: Entangled pair, 1,000 shots, ideal result: about 500 '00' and 500 '11'. Real device: 470 '00', 455 '11', 75 other. Error rate = 75 / 1,000 = 7.5%.
3.act: Run both circuits on a simulator and on one real device, 1,000 shots each, and tabulate the results.
3.std: Predictions written before runs; error rate computed; run table complete.

4.title: Cost a proof-of-concept project
4.intro: Quantum work is paid by the project. Price staff time, cloud hardware time and review, and show a buyer what they get.
pts: Variable cost per run: hardware time, extra staff review and reporting.
Fixed cost per month: tools, insurance, workspace, training and a share of the lead's time.
Offer a fixed-price study (for example 6 weeks) with a clear deliverable: a verdict, a baseline comparison and a plan.
Add 15% contingency because hardware queues and noise slow the schedule.
4.ex: Study price 2,400 per run-package; variable cost 900; margin 1,500 (63%). Fixed cost 7,000 a month is covered by about 5 packages. Teaching figures in CAD.
4.act: Build the cost sheet and compute break-even; show a case where only 3 packages sell.
4.std: Units and currency shown; three cases; arithmetic checked.

5.title: Operate the lab and keep records
5.intro: Good quantum work is repeatable work. Records make results believable.
pts: Record device, software version, calibration date, shots and random seed for every run.
Re-run any surprising result three times before you report it.
Keep a model of 'expected versus observed' for each circuit and flag drift over time.
Control access to cloud accounts and rotate keys; never paste keys into notes.
5.ex: Weekly page: 12 runs, 2 surprising, both repeated, one traced to a device recalibration; action: add calibration date to the run table.
5.act: Keep a 4-week run log and one weekly page.
5.std: Every run has all six fields; surprises are repeated.

6.title: Explain it and win a first client
6.intro: Buyers fund what they understand. Learn to explain quantum value in plain words with numbers.
pts: Use the answer-first form: result, reason, risk, next step.
Never promise advantage you have not shown; show a measured comparison with the best classical method.
Offer a no-regret first step: a two-week screen of the client's problems.
Partner with a university group or industry cluster for credibility and access to hardware.
6.ex: Pitch: 'We screened six scheduling problems; two may benefit from quantum-inspired methods now. We propose a six-week study with a stop point after week two.'
6.act: Give a five-minute explanation to a non-expert and collect three written questions.
6.std: Listener can repeat the verdict and the next step.

7.title: Handle security, ethics and trust
7.intro: Quantum advances create real risks as well as benefits.
pts: Data stolen today may be decrypted later; help clients inventory what must stay secret for ten years or more.
Plan the move to quantum-safe encryption: list systems, rank by life of data, test, replace in stages.
Be honest in marketing: do not claim speed-ups that you have not measured.
Include researchers and users from many backgrounds when you choose test problems.
7.ex: Inventory row: 'Customer records | secret for 25 years | high risk | pilot quantum-safe key exchange in test system by Q3'.
7.act: Write a one-page quantum-safe inventory for a fictional clinic.
7.std: Each system has a data life and a migration step.

8.title: Run a pilot study and plan growth
8.intro: A six-week pilot with a real client proves your process.
pts: Agree scope, a deliverable and a stop rule in writing.
Report weekly: tried, learned, next.
Close with a verdict, evidence and a recommendation, even if the verdict is 'not yet'.
Plan 12 months: three milestones, funding sources and a hiring plan.
8.ex: Stop rule: 'If after week 2 no problem passes the screen, we stop and refund the unused part.' Outcome: one problem passes; study continues.
8.act: Run a pilot on a sample problem and present the review.
8.std: Review includes a verdict, baseline comparison and a 12-month plan.

quiz: Name three problem families where quantum methods are studied.
Simulating molecules and materials, optimising or searching large option sets, and some cryptography.
What does a 'shot' mean?
One run of a circuit ending in a measurement; many shots give counts.
How do you compute the hardware error rate?
Unexpected counts divided by total shots.
Why check export rules before sharing designs?
Strategic technology can need a federal permit to leave the country.
Why re-run a surprising result?
To rule out noise or drift before reporting it.
What should a pitch avoid?
Promising advantage you have not measured against the best classical method.
Why inventory long-life secrets now?
Data stolen today may be decrypted later by quantum computers.
What belongs in a run record?
Device, software version, calibration date, shots, seed and result.
What is a no-regret first step for a client?
A short screen of their problems with a stop point.
What must a pilot agree before it starts?
Scope, deliverable and a stop rule.
